routes.description: Establish reflective Christianity as credible through a cumulative case from philosophical reasoning, scriptural and experiential considerations, and resurrection evidence, while limiting skeptical inferences from evil, disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive considerations provide reasonable warrant for Christianity and the negative considerations neither render its core claims unlikely nor defeat the cumulative case when assessed together.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative positive case and the answers to skeptical objections to the conclusion that reflective Christianity remains credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments can provide discriminating support for theism despite uncertainty about premises, divine motivations, and evidential partitioning.
Show that revelation, religious experience, and resurrection considerations supply warrant for distinctively Christian claims rather than generic theism alone.
Show that evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and moral failure do not outweigh or defeat the positive cumulative case.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify when cognitive limits and consequential complexity legitimately restrict skeptical likelihood judgments without indiscriminately defeating positive arguments.
Distinguish reasonable Christian credibility from certainty and explain why acknowledged disagreement need not require an atheistic conclusion.

routes.description: Establish skeptical atheism by challenging the predictive and explanatory force of the positive Christian considerations and presenting evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure as cumulative evidence against Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive arguments fail to make Christianity sufficiently probable and the negative considerations are better expected without the Christian account of God, revelation, resurrection, and transformation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the failure of the positive case and the cumulative skeptical evidence to the conclusion that Christianity is unlikely.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments, biblical beauty, religious experience, and resurrection evidence lack the claimed discriminatory or explanatory force.
Show that apparently preventable suffering and persistent religious confusion are less expected under the proposed Christian God than under naturalism.
Show that informed dissent and the observed moral record materially reduce confidence in Christianity's truth and transformative claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply naturalistic explanations for fine-tuning and resurrection data that avoid disputed assumptions about divine psychology or miraculous intervention.
Require consistent treatment of uncertainty, cognitive limitation, comparative expertise, and likelihood reasoning across positive and negative arguments.

sections.title: Philosophical Arguments, Fine-Tuning, and Divine Psychology
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether philosophical and fine-tuning arguments predict a life-permitting universe under theism or instead depend on uncertain premises, contested value theories, and arbitrary evidential partitions.

sections.title: Scripture, Religious Experience, and Reflective Warrant
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether biblical qualities and religious experience distinguish Christian revelation and justify reflective belief despite rival experiences, counterarguments, and disagreement.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether physical resurrection best explains the burial, appearances, and resulting bodily-resurrection belief or whether a naturalistic sequence explains the same evidence.

sections.title: Evil, Religious Disagreement, and Epistemic Limitation
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether suffering and failed or uneven revelation are improbable under Christianity, and whether appeals to consequential complexity or cognitive limits answer those inferences consistently.

sections.title: Expert Dissent, Rational Confidence, and Christian Moral Fruit
sections.rationale: This issue examines how interdisciplinary and specialist disagreement should constrain confidence and whether Christianity's claimed moral transformation generates unmet observable expectations relevant to credibility.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Philosophical arguments for God depend on numerous uncertain assumptions and speculative inferences about divine desires, motivations, and reasons for acting.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly solicits Fodor's reasons, and the uninterrupted answer uses first-person statements of his skeptical position.

response.rationale: This is a constructive challenge to the discriminatory force of philosophical theistic arguments, so no earlier opposing move is targeted.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central objection and identifies the disputed inferential dependency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The divine-psychology objection is recoverable and expressly qualified as applying to many arguments, though the covered argument class remains broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents a broad concern rather than a conclusive refutation and openly frames the underlying assumptions as uncertain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from dependence on speculative divine motivation to reduced argumentative force is coherent, with the degree of undercut left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated dependency is identifiable, but the excerpt supplies no representative survey showing how extensively philosophical arguments share it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central philosophical-warrant bridge by challenging the predictive premises used in theistic arguments.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: A perfectly good God's creative motivations can be grounded in moral value, so the goods enabled by conscious life make a life-permitting universe reasonably expected under theism.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue identifies himself as the author of a paper on divine psychology and presents its proposed moral-value inference before requesting a response.

components.text: Whether divine creative motivation can be non-speculatively inferred from perfect goodness and moral value.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive divine-motivation demand by proposing a moral-value rule, but it does not fully defend the rule or compare rival divine reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive component, placing it at the upper end of partial answers, but leaves the central warrant compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The moral-value proposal and fine-tuning application are recoverable, but the relevant range of creative contexts and competing goods is not fixed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Moral value plausibly bears on motivation, but the move advances an expectation without explicitly qualifying competing goods or creative options.

charity.alternative: Perfect goodness may permit many incomparable valuable creations rather than favoring a life-permitting universe like ours.
charity.decisiveQualification: Moral value supplies direction only if competing goods and divine reasons do not swamp the specified outcome.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The value-to-motivation-to-expectation chain is intelligible, but the bridge from greater value to sufficient comparative probability remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts its governing moral-value principle and the value of conscious life without defending the comparative probability warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable philosophical-warrant step by proposing a basis for expectations about divine creation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The proposal gives the skepticism a substantive answer but does not expressly handle the strongest many-goods qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that more morally valuable states are likelier to be actualized and that fine-tuned life enables moral goods.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Appealing to divine goodness does not make a universe like ours probable because the relevant theory of goodness is disputed and theism permits vastly many unlike creative possibilities.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor begins by identifying the proposal as a familiar approach and then develops sustained first-person objections to both its divine and moral premises.

components.text: Whether moral value makes a life-permitting universe like ours comparatively probable under theism.
Whether a defensible theory of goodness supports the proposed divine-motivation inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive comparative-probability inference and also addresses the moral-theory premise supporting that inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection clearly distinguishes disputed goodness assumptions from the swamping effect of other creative possibilities and acknowledges ongoing inquiry.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker reports being unconvinced rather than claiming impossibility and expressly acknowledges that the issue remains under exploration.

charity.alternative: A perfect being's reasons may privilege conscious moral goods enough to narrow the relevant creative possibilities.
charity.decisiveQualification: That privilege must make our universe or a suitably similar universe comparatively probable, not merely valuable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between value and comparative probability is clear, and the many-possibilities objection directly bears on the proposed likelihood.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rival-possibility warrant is plausible but remains largely conceptual, without a developed account of the relevant possibility space.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely attacks a central attempt to give fine-tuning discriminating philosophical support for theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the value-based proposal and targets its strongest remaining requirement: comparative probability among alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the proposed views fail to render our universe fairly probable because other creative possibilities swamp the comparison.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: When the laws of nature and psychophysical laws are included as background information, the relevant comparison narrows to universes under which fine-tuning remains expected if theism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue calls the preceding objection strong, introduces his published response, and specifies the two groups of laws his analysis conditions upon.

components.text: Whether the theistic comparison is swamped by a vast range of unlike creative possibilities.
Whether fine-tuning expectations still rely on an insufficiently constrained account of divine choice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive component and supplies a concrete narrowing device, but leaves the legitimacy of that device unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditioning proposal is clearly recoverable, though its evidential status as legitimate background information is only implicitly assumed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional expectation follows only if the selected laws may properly be held fixed, a material caveat not stated in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Treating our natural and psychophysical laws as background may arbitrarily condition away much of what needs explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The narrowed comparison helps only if the laws are independently admissible background rather than selected evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies no independent warrant for fixing the actual natural and psychophysical laws before assessing fine-tuning.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central philosophical-warrant bridge through a proposed fine-tuning likelihood comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the broad possibility problem but does not engage the strongest objection to its evidential partition.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly conditions on our natural and psychophysical laws and claims that fine-tuning is then expected under theism.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: The literary beauty and cultural importance of scripture do not establish divine inspiration because no defensible baseline distinguishes inspired texts from impressive human literature or rival scriptures.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained answer follows Donahue's question and is delivered in Fodor's skeptical first-person voice.

components.text: Whether conditioning on actual laws legitimately supports the fine-tuning likelihood comparison.
Whether moral value supplies a warranted comparative expectation about divine creation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that beauty does not establish inspiration without a baseline, a proportionate defeater claim rather than an excessive conclusion.

charity.alternative: Exceptional literary beauty could still be evidence of inspiration even without a perfectly objective literary metric.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its discriminatory force requires comparison with impressive human and rival religious texts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The missing-baseline objection follows directly from the need to distinguish inspired literature from impressive human or rival religious works.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the claimed discriminatory force of scriptural beauty within the positive Christian case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response allows that scripture may be impressive while accurately identifying the comparative requirement for divine attribution.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes the parallel Quranic beauty claim and asks for criteria and comparison texts establishing an appropriate baseline.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Calling Christian religious experience self-authenticating does not resolve its epistemic weakness because it provides no reliable way to distinguish Christian revelation from rival religious experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer directly follows Donahue's presentation of Craig's position and consistently expresses Fodor's skeptical epistemology.

components.text: Whether the selected background laws legitimately narrow the fine-tuning comparison.
Whether moral value adequately constrains divine creative motivation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It materially bears on the cumulative positive case but remains a relevant nonanswer to the schema-exposed earlier targets.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accommodates the first-person proposal while retaining the central reliability challenge posed by rival experiences.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that experiential recognition available only after the experience cannot be explained or reliably distinguished across claimants.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Belief in God may be properly basic when grounded in coherent and undefeated direct experience of divine reality, analogously to ordinary warranted trust in the external world.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly describes his own enduring experience of God while presenting Plantinga-style reformed epistemology.

components.text: Whether direct experience can warrant belief despite the inability to provide an outsider-accessible discriminator.
Whether rival religious experiences defeat otherwise properly basic Christian experiential belief.

response.rationale: The external-world analogy contacts the demand for first-person warrant, but it does not resolve the decisive rival-experience and defeater-discrimination component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary warrant component but leaves the strongest rival-experience component unanswered, placing it midrange among partial answers.

precisionFindings.rationale: The properly basic experiential claim and external-world analogy are recoverable, but the required coherence and undefeatedness conditions remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move modestly claims that belief can be justified, while acknowledging complexity through analogy rather than asserting indefeasible certainty.

charity.alternative: Rival incompatible experiences may operate as defeaters even if direct experience ordinarily supplies prima facie warrant.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy works only if Christian experience remains coherent and undefeated after rival claims are considered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports religious experience as warrant for Christian belief, an indispensable positive Christian-evidence step.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly presents prima facie experiential warrant but omits the strongest defeater qualification raised by the opponent.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes Plantinga-style properly basic belief and compares direct experience of God with warranted trust in the external world.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: A temporary reburial, bereavement experiences, memory-shaping biases, and socialization can jointly explain sincere early Christian resurrection belief without a literal bodily resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor identifies the account as his RHBS model and systematically explains each naturalistic component in the first person.

response.rationale: The naturalistic resurrection model is relevant to the positive Christian case but does not contact the experiential-warrant demand in the available target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is substantive contrary material on another evidential component, making it a relevant nonanswer to the legal earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed sequence and its naturalistic aim are clear, and the speaker presents it as a possible explanatory model rather than established history.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The model is offered as a way the belief could emerge and is expressly grounded in existing psychological, sociological, and historical ideas.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The multi-stage naturalistic sequence is internally compatible and potentially explanatory, though several causal transitions remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It appeals to established disciplinary concepts but the excerpt provides little specific evidence for their joint application to early Christianity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary naturalistic-alternatives bridge by supplying a concrete resurrection-belief model.

representationalCharity.rationale: The selected excerpt introduces the naturalistic model without yet comparing a developed strongest resurrection alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies the RHBS model as combining psychology, sociology, and historical case study to explain sincere early resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Jewish expectations do not uniquely favor a resurrection inference, while collective experiences and a perceived empty tomb could produce bodily-resurrection belief under a naturalistic account.
moves.attributionBasis: The response directly addresses Donahue's Craig-style objection and restates distinctive elements of Fodor's naturalistic model.

components.text: Whether direct experience can constitute properly basic belief despite potential defeaters.

response.rationale: The move develops resurrection-specific expectations and naturalistic mechanisms but does not answer the earlier experiential epistemology claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It bears on Christianity's evidential case while remaining a relevant nonanswer to the sole legally exposed earlier target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empty-tomb and appearance components are clearly specified as shared explananda under competing resurrection and naturalistic accounts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that the same evidence is compatible with its model without claiming that compatibility alone establishes historical probability.

charity.alternative: Bodily-resurrection belief is especially expected if the appearances were genuinely physical and the tomb was empty.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those data do not uniquely favor resurrection if a naturalistic model independently predicts both an empty tomb and physical interpretation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Showing that both accounts predict the cited evidence coherently undercuts uniqueness, though it does not by itself establish comparative superiority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The model specifies relevant mechanisms but does not provide enough historical or psychological support to establish their comparative likelihood.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary tier by directly offering an alternative explanation of resurrection belief and its evidential features.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the resurrection advocate's central data while directly disputing their claimed explanatory uniqueness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Fodor's account, like Craig's, includes an empty tomb and appearances interpreted as bodily or physical.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Physical appearances of Jesus better explain both the reported phenomenological character of the appearances and the disciples' specifically bodily interpretation of their experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: Donahue explicitly frames the passage as advocacy for Craig and develops the resurrection explanation against Fodor's characterization.

components.text: Whether the naturalistic account explains the appearances' phenomenological character and specifically bodily interpretation.
Whether hallucination and social-memory mechanisms adequately explain the reported appearance narratives.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that physical appearances better explain both phenomenology and bodily interpretation, contacting the naturalistic model's decisive explanatory demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the decisive comparative-explanation component and also challenges a central mechanism in the broader sequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed explanatory advantage is clear, though the relevant narrative set and exact phenomenological features are not specified in the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims a better explanation without supplying an explicit reliability qualification for the reported appearance narratives.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic collective experiences plus an empty tomb could lead sincere witnesses to a bodily interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: That account must also explain the reported phenomenological features rather than merely the resulting doctrinal belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Physical appearance would coherently explain physical-seeming reports and bodily interpretation, though the inference depends on report reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies specific explananda but offers no detailed documentation or comparison of the narratives and naturalistic mechanisms.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports distinctively Christian resurrection evidence by arguing for the physical-appearance explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly preserves the naturalistic proposal and presses a legitimate additional explanatory requirement, albeit without detailed comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says hallucinations would not explain the appearances' phenomenological characteristics and that resurrection better explains experiences of Jesus alive.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Extensive apparently preventable suffering is unexpected if a perfectly good and powerful God created the world to realize morally valuable well-being.
moves.attributionBasis: Fodor begins the requested explanation of the problem of evil and develops it continuously through the delivered context boundary.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents apparently preventable suffering as comparative evidence against a perfectly good and powerful creator.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly states a central skeptical likelihood argument and identifies its theological conditioning assumptions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential claim is recoverable and explicitly conditioned on traditional theism and particular views of God's nature and creative reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances an evidential likelihood claim while expressly acknowledging its contingency on the proposed divine nature and purposes.

charity.alternative: God may permit suffering for morally sufficient goods inaccessible from the local human perspective.
charity.decisiveQualification: The evidential argument concerns the extensive apparently preventable pattern, not proof that no sufficient reason is possible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the specified goodness and creative-purpose assumptions, the inference from preventable suffering to reduced expectation is coherent and appropriately conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The empirical pattern is recognizable, but the excerpt does not develop representative cases or a full comparison with proposed justifying goods.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central world-evidence bridge through the principal evidential problem-of-evil comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move appropriately frames the case as conditional evidence rather than a deductive claim that excludes every possible divine reason.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditions the problem of evil on traditional theism, God's reasons for creating, and the realization of morally good states.

moves.speaker: Miles K. Donahue
moves.proposition: Because historical consequences are deeply interconnected and compound beyond human prediction, only an omniscient mind could reliably compare the total outcomes relevant to apparently gratuitous evil.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies the skeptical-theist view he finds most plausible, names its consequential-complexity rationale, develops it, and asks for a response.

components.text: Whether humans can reliably classify apparently preventable suffering as lacking outweighing total consequences.
Whether the observed suffering pattern remains unlikely given unknown long-run consequences.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive likelihood judgment by arguing that compounding historical consequences exceed human comparative capacity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the skeptical inference's epistemic premise, though it does not resolve whether local evidence retains residual force.

precisionFindings.rationale: The compounding-consequences claim, temporal mechanism, and omniscience requirement are stated clearly and presented as plausible rather than certain.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker explicitly says the claim is plausible on its face and does not present consequential complexity as a demonstrated necessity.

charity.alternative: Even without total consequential knowledge, humans may reasonably judge some suffering to be antecedently unlikely under perfect goodness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Complexity defeats that judgment only if unknown consequences are sufficiently connected to the relevant divine permission decision.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Compounding divergence plausibly limits total-outcome comparisons, but the bridge from limited knowledge to broad suspension of evidential judgment remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The butterfly-effect style mechanism is plausible but unsupported by specific evidence that morally sufficient consequences attach to the relevant sufferings.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central world-evidence bridge by challenging the reliability of apparently gratuitous-evil judgments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses total-outcome comparison but does not fully preserve the strongest modest evidential inference from local suffering.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says small event changes compound into divergent histories and that only an omniscient or near-omniscient mind could compare them.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Geographic religious contingency and deep Christian doctrinal disagreement are more expected under naturalism than under a God who intends to reveal beliefs and practices to humanity.
moves.attributionBasis: Following an explicit topic transition and request for the skeptical argument, the speaker gives a sustained first-person explanation of two levels of religious disagreement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a direct central likelihood comparison and identifies two concrete forms of religious confusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central world-evidence bridge by challenging the expected clarity and reach of Christian revelation.

moves.attributionBasis: The speaker says the problem has core plausibility, identifies what he considers Christianity's best response, and then states a secondary cumulative-case response.

components.text: Whether religious disagreement has a determinable low likelihood under Christianity.
Whether disagreement evidence can be outweighed by the remaining cumulative Christian case.
Whether consequential complexity similarly limits likelihood judgments about evil.

moves.proposition: Broad philosophical opinion is weak evidence against theism because most philosophers lack specialist knowledge of contemporary philosophy of religion, while specialist opinion is affected by selection effects.

moves.attributionBasis: The turn agrees that confidence in theism should move downward while objecting to treating disagreement as support for atheism, which coheres with Donahue's pro position.

components.text: Whether informed peer disagreement requires moderation of confidence in theism.
Whether such moderation supports an all-things-considered probability below one-half or atheistic belief.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the confidence-moderation demand and then limits its consequence, distinguishing downward adjustment from positive support for atheism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both the accepted moderation component and the disputed inference from moderation to atheistic belief.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes reduced confidence, extreme certainty, a final probability below one-half, and belief that God does not exist.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly concedes downward movement and complexity while resisting only a stronger posterior conclusion not established by disagreement alone.

charity.alternative: Disagreement can combine with independent skeptical evidence and thereby contribute to a posterior below one-half.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply's limitation applies to disagreement alone, not to an all-evidence cumulative skeptical case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between lowering confidence and crossing the belief threshold is explicit and logically sound, absent further magnitude assumptions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual threshold distinction is well defended, though no quantitative account establishes how much moderation is actually warranted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central social-epistemic inference while conceding that informed dissent constrains confidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The distinction is fair, though the wording about a final probability risks compressing the opponent's broader cumulative-evidence position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts downward confidence adjustment because experts disagree but denies that disagreement itself establishes atheism or a ten-percent posterior.

moves.speaker: James Fodor
moves.proposition: Christian claims that divine indwelling morally transforms believers generate an observable expectation that Christians should display better moral conduct than the historical and contemporary record appears to show.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker introduces the final skeptical consideration, characterizes it as an objection from Christian moral fruits, and develops it in the first person as Fodor's argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move derives an observable moral-conduct expectation from Christian claims of divine indwelling and transformation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it articulates a central empirical test, though the selected evidence only begins developing the comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The transformation expectation is recoverable, but the relevant Christian population, comparison group, and measure of moral improvement remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker calls the claim potentially and indirectly testable, appropriately limiting the strength of the empirical proposal.

charity.alternative: Christian transformation may be gradual, uneven, or relative to a believer's counterfactual conduct rather than population superiority.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection needs a specified transformation claim and comparison before observed misconduct becomes strong contrary evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A claimed transforming indwelling plausibly creates observable expectations, but the bridge to aggregate comparative conduct needs scope conditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a testable implication but the excerpt supplies no representative behavioral evidence, baseline, or controlled comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the social-epistemic case by testing Christianity's claimed transformative moral fruits against observation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes indirect testing but does not yet incorporate the strongest counterfactual and population-selection qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt characterizes moral fruits and divine transformation as potentially testable, though not directly, through expected believer conduct.
